extracted.intended_audience: writers, students, and general readers interested in narrative theory, screenwriting, and literary analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of what a plot is and how plots are structured, including definitions (plot vs story), formalist distinctions (fabula/syuzhet), classical and modern dramatic structures (Aristotle, Freytag, three-act), plot devices, and practical advice on outlines and summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as cause-and-effect sequence (Forster)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is the cause-and-effect relationship between events in a story (e.g., 'The king died, and then the queen died of grief' is a plot; mere sequential events without causal linkage are only a story).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only include events that move the action or have consequences; memorable scenes that do not influence subsequent events (e.g., Rose on the railing in Titanic; Han Solo frozen in carbonite in The Empire Strikes Back) are not part of the plot. Teri Shaffer Yamada: focus on 'major events that move the action in a narrative.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabula vs Syuzhet (story vs plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fabula is the chronological ordering of events (what happened); syuzhet is the selection and ordering of those events as presented by the author — a unique sequence of discourse which may be non-chronological.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Syuzhet can reorder or 'defamiliarize' fabula (temporal displacements, digressions, causal disruptions) to alter perception — e.g., Tristram Shandy uses temporal displacement and digression as defamiliarization (Shklovsky).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must highlight significant incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is built of significant events — incidents that are significant because they have important consequences for what follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude incidental actions (e.g., taking a shower) that do not affect later events; focus on actions, feelings, thoughts, or speech that change outcomes (Ansen Dibell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-act structure (set-up, confrontation, resolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: A common plot structure especially in Europe and the European diaspora: three acts — the set-up (Act I), the confrontation (Act II), and the resolution (Act III), with acts connected by two plot points/turning points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often used for treatments when selling scripts; structure and how it is split can vary by ethnicity, region, time period, and genre (Syd Field attribution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotelian unity and components
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle: a play should imitate a single whole action with a beginning, middle and end; he emphasized complication and denouement, the importance of discovery, and that reversal and recognition are key scene types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversals should be necessary and probable results of prior events (properly set up). Aristotle ranked components' importance (Chorus, Events, Diction, Character, Spectacle) and argued against episodic plots; morality and the teaching function (pity, fear, suffering) are central in tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freytag's five-part dramatic pyramid
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Freytag the plot consists of five parts: Exposition (introduction), Rising action, Climax (turning point), Falling action (return or fall), and Catastrophe/Denouement/Resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freytag adds three crises/moments (exciting force, tragic force, force of final suspense). Definitions: exposition sets setting/mood/characters; rise builds to greatest interest; climax changes protagonist's fate; return/falling should keep characters and scenes limited; catastrophe should be foreshadowed to avoid non sequitur. Freytag emphasizes emotional contrast and tension; some components (tragic force, final suspense) are optional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposition delivery methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposition can be conveyed through dialogues, flashbacks, characters' asides, background details, in-universe media, or a narrator telling backstory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these devices to supply necessary background and backstory without interrupting narrative flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot devices vs dramatic technique
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot device is a means of advancing the plot (motivating characters, creating urgency, or resolving difficulty), contrasted with dramatic technique where characters take action for well-developed reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common plot devices include deus ex machina, MacGuffin, red herring, and Chekhov's gun. Prefer dramatic technique (character-driven causes) over cheap devices (e.g., sudden cavalry arrival) unless intentionally employed for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot outline as functional blueprint
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot outline is a prose telling of a story (often a one-page synopsis) that can be turned into a screenplay; in comics this stage ('roughs' or nēmu) breaks the story into panel flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main goals of roughs: lay out flow of panels across a page, ensure the story builds suspense, work out points of view/camera angles/character positions, and serve as basis for the next polished stage. In fiction, an outline lists scenes (events, characters, setting) to create a cause-and-effect backbone and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot summary conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot summary is a brief description explaining what happens in a work; it should refer to the author and title and is usually no more than a paragraph long while summarizing main points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep summaries concise and focused on main events rather than incidental scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: A-Plot (primary driving storyline)
rubrics_metrics.description: An A-Plot is the plotline that drives the story — the line that forces most of the action (term commonly used in cinema and television).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An A-Plot may not always be the most important thematically, but it typically compels the bulk of events and other plotlines (B-plots, subplots) orbit it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denouement and catharsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Denouement (dénouement) comprises events from the end of the falling action to the actual ending scene where conflicts are resolved, normality restored, and the reader experiences catharsis or release of tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Etymology: 'to untie' — ensure complexities are unraveled; resolution should feel earned and provide emotional release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreshadowing and setup for reversals/catastrophe
rubrics_metrics.description: Major turning points (reversals, catastrophe) should be properly set up/foreshadowed so they do not appear as non sequitur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freytag warns against sparing the hero unjustifiably and recommends foreshadowing to make catastrophic outcomes plausible; set-up makes reversals feel necessary and probable (Aristotle/Freytag guidance).
